text: DOTS programme may limit the development of multi- drug-resistant tuberculosis, different strategies are re- quired in areas where multidrug resistance is already es- tablished. These have been formulated by the WHO in the DOTS-plus strategy for countries with well functioning tuberculosis control programmes.10 Patients with multidrug-resistant tuberculosis and those who relapse after completing the WHO standard treatment regimens should receive a DOTS-plus regimen, which in- cludes second-line antituberculous drugs. Drugs used in the treatment of drug-resistant tuberculosis are generally less effective and more toxic than standard therapy and need to be taken daily. They include the aminoglycosides (amikacin, capreomycin, and kanamycin), aminosali- cylates, cycloserine, ethionamide, fluoroquinolones (cip- rofloxacin, levofloxacin, and ofloxacin), protionamide, and terizidone. The DOTS-plus regimen should consist of at least 3 or 4 oral drugs plus an injectable aminoglycoside, to which the patient has not been exposed and which do not share cross-resistance with drugs given previously. These drugs should be given under direct observation for at least 6 months, and followed by a continuation phase of 12 to 18 months with at least 3 drugs.5,8 Cross-resistance between rifampicin and rifabutin is common and rifabutin is therefore not recommended as a second-line drug. Cross-resistance among aminoglycosides is uncommon, while cross-resistance is variable within the fluoroquinolo- nes. Cross-resistance is complete between ethionamide and protionamide, and between cycloserine and teriz- idone. Where available, M. tuberculosis resistance testing should be performed to guide the choice of therapy. Single drugs should never be added to a failing regimen. Extensively drug-resistant tuberculosis (XDR-TB) is de- fined as tuberculosis that is resistant to isoniazid and rif- ampicin and also resistant to fluoroquinolones and at least one of three injectable second-line drugs (amikacin, capre- omycin, or kanamycin).11 XDR-TB can develop when the second-line drugs are misused or mismanaged and by early 2006 cases were being reported from every region in the world.12 A report from the KwaZulu-Natal province of South Africa highlighted the risk for rapid death in HIV- infected persons with extensively-drug resistant tuberculo- sis.13 In this local case series, all but one of 53 patients died, and where the date of death could be confirmed the median survival was 16 days from the time of diagnosis. • Children and infants can be treated with regimens sim- ilar to adults but with appropriate dose adjustments for age or body-weight.4-7 While ethambutol is not usually given to young children because of the perceived difficulty in de- tecting ocular toxicity
